Two days later, Jae-won noticed that the lunch-set price on the print file was ₩9,000 instead of ₩9,500. Three hundred menus had already been printed. Ms. Park said they could use price stickers for the weekend, but Jae-won heard her tired voice as proof she regretted hiring him. He paid for a corrected print run himself and spent Friday night checking the matching Instagram graphics, zooming in until the letters blurred. He tried taking a walk to photograph old shop signs near his apartment and starting a co-op game with a friend, but kept returning to the files. By Sunday, he was exhausted and ashamed, despite having fixed the error.

name: Choi Jun-ho
occupation: Middle-school math instructor at a neighborhood hagwon in Daejeon
topic: A mistake in a math handout and the parent complaint that followed.
core_concern: He worries that his careful, dependable self is slipping under the strain of teaching and caring for his parents. Beneath the complaint, he feels hopeless and frightened by how familiar it feels after a dark period in 2022.
background: Jun-ho teaches middle-school math at a neighborhood hagwon in Daejeon. On April 17, he handed out a practice sheet for an upcoming school exam with an incorrect answer key. A parent posted a photo of it in the class KakaoTalk chat, and the hagwon director asked him to send a correction before his 4 p.m. class. He did, but felt exposed and kept checking the chat for more complaints. That morning he had taken his father to a follow-up appointment at Chungnam National University Hospital; the corrected sheet was still on his desk beside an untouched convenience-store kimbap when he got home. He has tried rechecking every handout and telling the director he is fine, but the mistake keeps replaying in his head. Since late March, difficult evenings have left him feeling hopeless.

name: Yoon Jae-won
occupation: Second-year student at a middle school in Busan
topic: A disappointing math-hagwon test and another class added to Jae-won's schedule.
core_concern: He worries that school pressure getting to him this much makes him weak or dramatic.
background: On Friday, March 13, Jae-won scored 71 out of 100 on a diagnostic test at his math hagwon in Busan's Yeonsan-dong. He had expected to do better and felt embarrassed when he folded the score sheet into his backpack beside a half-finished futsal video edit. The next evening, his parents added a Thursday class that runs until 9:30 p.m. His mother called it a head start for university; Jae-won heard it as proof that his effort did not count. He tried saying the extra class would leave no time for futsal or editing, but the conversation became an argument about his future. Since then he has been quieter at home. He still wants his parents to notice something is wrong, but worries they will think he is making excuses.

name: Lee Da-eun
occupation: Webtoon studio assistant at a small production studio in Nohyeong-dong, Jeju City; helps with panel cleanup, lettering, and episode preparation
topic: Da-eun cannot bring herself to review a disappointing timed studio assessment.
core_concern: She fears she is becoming a burden to her mother and that doing poorly at her June work review would make all her mother's patience and support feel wasted. She has been avoiding her mother too, because even an ordinary question about work makes her feel like a disappointment.
background: On May 9, Da-eun took a timed panel-cleanup and lettering assessment at the webtoon studio in Nohyeong-dong. She scored 62, down from 79 the month before, with a studio performance review approaching in June. She felt stunned on the bus home, then ashamed when her mother asked how it went while putting away groceries. Da-eun said only that it was difficult. The next day at the Jeju City library, she opened her marked-up assessment sheet but spent an hour rearranging her practice plan instead of checking her mistakes. She tried making a shorter revision list at home, but left that unfinished too. Now two days have passed, and the folded assessment sheet is still in her bag beside a library receipt. She has stopped replying to a studio team chat. She worries that her mother is carrying the household errands and expenses while she produces nothing to show for it. The score and the lost days hurt.

name: Shin Hee-won
occupation: Administrative assistant at a small packaging-design firm in Seoul, handling invoices, schedules, and client emails
topic: A corrected delivery mistake at work that Hee-won cannot stop replaying.
core_concern: Hee-won fears that needing reassurance after an already-fixed mistake makes her burdensome. She feels embarrassed and hurt at being dismissed.
background: This morning at a small packaging-design firm in Mapo, Hee-won arranged a courier for sample boxes going to a client's Seongsu showroom. She copied the old entrance from a previous request, noticed the mismatch when the courier called at 11:18, and corrected it. The boxes arrived before the client's 2 p.m. review, and her manager confirmed that nothing had been delayed. Hee-won felt briefly relieved, then embarrassed when a coworker brushed off her attempt to explain why she had been rattled. On the Line 2 ride home, she replayed both the mistake and her coworker's reaction. She has checked the delivery confirmation twice and drafted, but not sent, an apologetic KakaoTalk message to her manager. Now she is in her Mangwon studio with a triangle kimbap still unopened on the table. The delivery is resolved; what has not settled is the feeling that her worry is an inconvenience to other people.

name: Shin Ki-hyun
occupation: Stay-at-home parent managing the household and school-day routines for his two children
topic: An argument about school expenses and the work of managing the household.
core_concern: He feels hurt, not just worried about the spending. The argument has brought back the shame and hopelessness he remembers from a dark period in 2023. He worries that admitting this will make his spouse see him as incapable of caring for the children.
background: On March 18, 2026, Ki-hyun paid a 48,000-won school activity fee through the e-Alimi school notice app for his nine-year-old and renewed his twelve-year-old’s 260,000-won math hagwon enrollment. That evening, his spouse noticed both charges and asked why they had not discussed them first. Ki-hyun understood the concern about money, but felt that keeping track of notices, deadlines, and pickups had become invisible until a payment appeared. He defended the expenses, then apologized for his tone. He lay awake replaying the exchange while a damp taekwondo uniform hung over the bathroom door. They had already tried a shared expense spreadsheet and a Sunday check-in, but both fell away when the week got busy. He now has the numbers ready and wants a practical way to raise them, though another budget discussion feels inadequate. His spouse knows it happened, but they have rarely spoken about it since. What unsettles him is how familiar his sense of failure feels.

name: Hong Seo-jin
occupation: Travel consultant at a small travel agency near Geumchon Station in Paju, handling flight and package-tour bookings
topic: A disappointing booking-skills assessment and a difficult week at the agency.
core_concern: She worries that failing at the agency will confirm she has wasted her savings and her parents' patience. The pressure frightens her.
background: On March 10, Seo-jin took a monthly booking-skills assessment at the travel agency near Geumchon Station. Her average score was 62, down from 71 the previous month; the visa-documentation section was 45. She felt ashamed, especially because she recognized mistakes she had made before. For the next two days at the agency, she spent hours color-coding those mistakes instead of retrying the sample booking cases. At dinner on March 12, her father asked whether she had considered looking for a steadier office job. He meant it as a practical question, but she heard it as proof that he had lost confidence in her. She said she was fine, then took an evening walk and photographed the peeling blue sign outside a closed stationery shop. She has tried making a stricter work checklist and brushing off her parents' questions, but neither has eased the pressure. Now she is at her usual end-of-row desk, unable to start a practice booking. She has not told anyone how much the pressure frightens her. She feels frightened and ashamed.

name: Lee Bo-ra
occupation: Job seeker applying for junior operations coordinator roles at e-commerce companies in Seoul
topic: A rejection after an operations coordinator interview in Seoul.
core_concern: She worries that one spreadsheet mistake proves she is not capable of doing the jobs she applies for. She is especially ashamed that she cannot bring herself to update her carefully kept application tracker.
background: On March 17, Bo-ra traveled from Bucheon to Guro Digital Complex for an interview at a small e-commerce company. During a short spreadsheet exercise, she noticed too late that she had sorted a returns column incorrectly. She left feeling cautiously hopeful because the interviewer had asked when she could start. On March 19, a brief rejection email arrived while she was on Line 1. She read it beside a window fogged by someone’s takeaway coffee, then closed her application spreadsheet without recording the result. Her roommate thinks she is still waiting to hear back. Bo-ra has tried replaying the exercise to work out whether that mistake cost her the job, but it has only made her avoid the spreadsheet. She has not explained the whole search to her roommate. She is distressed and ashamed.

name: Choi Eun-sook
occupation: Senior public job program worker who tidies reading tables and restocks notices at a neighborhood library in Daegu three mornings a week
topic: A mistake with notices during her morning shift at the library.
core_concern: She worries that her age and carefulness are no longer enough, and that coworkers may see her as a burden and eventually stop giving her work. She feels embarrassed and worried, given what the job means to her.
background: On her Tuesday morning shift at Daegu Metropolitan Suseong Library, Eun-sook restocked the reading-room notice stand with flyers for a spring reading event. Near noon, a coworker noticed that she had used an older stack with the wrong registration date. Eun-sook replaced them before leaving; the coworker said it was an easy mistake, and the supervisor simply reminded her to check dates. Still, she felt embarrassed all the way home on the bus. On Thursday she checked every notice twice, then apologized to the coworker again, who seemed puzzled by the apology. She has tried telling herself that no one was harmed, but she keeps picturing someone deciding she is too slow for the three-mornings-a-week job. Her program wages help cover rent and utilities, and the library is one of the few places where she feels useful. This small mistake has stayed with her.

name: Lim Han-na
occupation: Social welfare major at Kyonggi University’s Suwon campus
topic: A disappointing practice-exam score and an awkward dinner with her mother.
core_concern: She feels the exam score is not the only problem. She is frightened by how much an old crisis has been on her mind.
background: Han-na is majoring in social welfare at Kyonggi University’s Suwon campus and studies at a study café in Suwon. On March 14, 2026, her practice-exam average fell from 78 to 68, with social welfare policy dropping to 55. She copied the missed questions into her notebook, but by Monday she was still rereading the score instead of reviewing them. At dinner, her mother asked whether she should consider office work again if her studies do not go well. Han-na knows her mother worries about their grocery costs, yet heard the question as a loss of faith in her. She tried making a new study timetable and calling her friend Min-ji on the walk home; neither quieted the worry. She even photographed a neighborhood cat sitting beside a crushed milk carton, then felt guilty for stopping. She is now at the study café, struggling to concentrate.

name: Jang Dan-bi
occupation: Second-year student at a public middle school in Daejeon
topic: Being left out of lunch plans and dreading the school cafeteria.
core_concern: She worries that snapping at Minji makes her look needy or mean.
background: Dan-bi is a second-year student at a public middle school in Daejeon. On March 12, she saw three friends arranging where to sit at lunch in their group chat without asking her. She felt embarrassed but told herself it might happen only once. On March 16, they did it again. She asked Minji whether there was room at their table; Minji replied, “idk,” and Dan-bi spent the evening rereading it instead of practicing a pop song on her borrowed keyboard. On March 18, Dan-bi stood in the cafeteria holding her tray while the friends waved another classmate into the last open seat. The metal chopsticks kept sliding against the tray as she looked for somewhere else to sit. Later, she snapped at Minji in the hallway, asking why sitting with her had become a problem. Minji said she was making it a big deal and walked away. Dan-bi has already tried asking directly and acting as though nothing happened; neither made lunch feel easier. She is now dreading tomorrow’s lunch and feels both hurt by the exclusion and ashamed of how sharply she spoke.

name: Kim Eun-young
occupation: Owner and sole tailor at a clothing alterations shop in Ssangyong-dong, Cheonan
topic: A canceled school-uniform alterations order and a difficult evening at the shop.
core_concern: She fears the hopelessness she remembers from a dark period before is returning. She fears being seen as a bad mother.
background: On Monday, a parent from her daughter’s school brought in six uniforms for alterations. Eun-young stayed late marking the hems with blue tailor’s chalk, relieved that the work would cover a good part of this month’s shop rent.
